exercises.prompt: Which past tense do Germans actually say out loud about yesterday?
options: Both are equally common in speech.
exercises.explain: In spoken German the Perfekt is the ordinary past. The Präteritum survives in writing, and in speech for sein, haben and the modals.

exercises.prompt: Er ___ letzte Woche nach Hamburg gefahren.
exercises.explain: Verbs of movement from A to B take sein. fahren, gehen, kommen, fliegen, reisen — all sein.

exercises.prompt: Ich ___ die ganze Nacht geschlafen.
exercises.explain: No movement and no change of state, so haben — even though English says "I was asleep".

exercises.prompt: Ich habe gestern gekauft ein Buch.
exercises.fix: Ich habe gestern ein Buch gekauft.
exercises.explain: The Partizip II goes to the very end of the clause. Everything else — object, time, place — comes before it.

exercises.prompt: Wir haben das Zimmer ___. (aufräumen)
exercises.explain: A separable verb puts the ge- *inside*: auf + ge + räumt. Never in front.

exercises.prompt: Sie hat lange in Berlin ___. (studieren)
exercises.explain: Verbs ending in -ieren take no ge- at all: studiert, telefoniert, funktioniert.

exercises.prompt: What is the Plusquamperfekt actually for?
options: Marking the earlier of two past events.
Making a past event sound more formal.
Talking about the very distant past.
exercises.explain: It is relative, not remote: it only means "before that other past thing". On its own, in a sentence with no second past event, it has nothing to be earlier than.

exercises.prompt: Nachdem wir gegessen ___, sind wir spazieren gegangen.
exercises.explain: nachdem takes the earlier event, so Plusquamperfekt: hatten gegessen. The main clause then goes Perfekt or Präteritum.

exercises.prompt: ___ ich das Haus verließ, hatte ich schon gefrühstückt.
exercises.explain: The breakfast came first, so the clause with the *later* event takes bevor. Swap the conjunction and you swap which event was earlier.

exercises.prompt: Nachdem er ankam, ging er sofort ins Bett.
exercises.fix: Nachdem er angekommen war, ging er sofort ins Bett.
exercises.explain: nachdem needs the Plusquamperfekt. With a plain Präteritum the sentence loses the ordering that nachdem exists to state.

exercises.prompt: Sie ___ schon gegangen, als ich ankam.
exercises.explain: gehen takes sein, so the Plusquamperfekt is war gegangen — the same auxiliary the Perfekt would use, one tense further back.

exercises.prompt: Build the earlier event:
exercises.explain: Nebensatz first: the finite hatte goes to the end of its own clause, and the main clause then starts with its verb.

exercises.prompt: How do Germans usually talk about tomorrow?
options: Präsens plus a time word: „Ich fahre morgen nach Köln.“
Futur I, always: „Ich werde morgen nach Köln fahren.“
Either — they are used equally often.
exercises.explain: This is the fact English speakers most often miss. The present tense with a time expression *is* the normal German future; Futur I is for prediction, promise or emphasis.

exercises.prompt: Es ___ morgen bestimmt regnen.
exercises.explain: A prediction — that is exactly what Futur I is for. Note it is wird, not will: German *will* means *wants*.

exercises.prompt: Ich will dich morgen anrufen, versprochen.
exercises.fix: Ich werde dich morgen anrufen, versprochen.
exercises.explain: The commonest false friend in the language. „Ich will“ is „I want to“; the English *will* is werden.

exercises.prompt: Nächstes Jahr ___ wir nach Wien ziehen.
exercises.explain: wir → werden, with the infinitive at the end of the clause.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is a guess about *now*, not the future?
options: Er wird wohl im Stau stehen.
Er wird morgen im Stau stehen.
exercises.explain: Futur I plus wohl expresses present probability — "he is probably stuck in traffic". The tense is future; the meaning is not.

exercises.prompt: Build the promise:
exercises.explain: werden takes position two and the infinitive goes to the end. Everything else sits in the middle.

exercises.prompt: What is the passive actually for?
options: Saying what happens when who does it does not matter.
exercises.explain: It moves the action to the front and the doer out of the way — which is why notices, recipes and instructions are full of it.

exercises.prompt: Hier ___ Deutsch gesprochen.
exercises.explain: werden + Partizip II. „ist gesprochen“ would describe a state, not what happens here.

exercises.prompt: Die Formulare ___ am Eingang ausgefüllt.
exercises.explain: The subject is plural — die Formulare — so werden. The Partizip never changes.

exercises.prompt: Das Haus wird ___ einem Architekten geplant.
exercises.explain: von names the person or agent doing it; durch names the means or cause — „durch ein Erdbeben zerstört“.

exercises.prompt: Das Zimmer wird jeden Tag putzen.
exercises.fix: Das Zimmer wird jeden Tag geputzt.
exercises.explain: werden takes the Partizip II, not the infinitive. With the infinitive the sentence reads as a future active — "the room will clean".

exercises.prompt: Make it passive: „Man repariert das Auto.“ → „Das Auto ___ repariert.“
exercises.explain: man-sentences are the easiest to convert: drop man, and the object becomes the subject.

exercises.prompt: Die Brücke ist letztes Jahr renoviert ___.
exercises.explain: In the passive the Partizip of werden is worden, never geworden. geworden belongs to the full verb — „Er ist Arzt geworden“.

exercises.prompt: Der Vertrag muss heute noch unterschrieben ___.
exercises.explain: With a modal the passive ends in the bare infinitive werden, and the modal carries the person.

exercises.prompt: Das Fenster ist gestern repariert geworden.
exercises.fix: Das Fenster ist gestern repariert worden.
exercises.explain: The single commonest passive slip at B1. Passive → worden; becoming something → geworden.

exercises.prompt: Which one says the window *is currently in a repaired state*?
exercises.explain: sein + Partizip is the Zustandspassiv — the result. The second reports the event, the third reports it happening now.

exercises.prompt: Build the passive with a modal:
exercises.explain: Modal at position two, then Partizip, then werden right at the end — two verbs stacked at the clause end.

exercises.prompt: Perfekt passive: „Der Brief wird geschrieben.“ → „Der Brief ist geschrieben ___.“
exercises.explain: wird → ist … worden.

exercises.prompt: A German notice says „Der Laden ist geschlossen.“ What does it tell you?
options: The shop is shut right now — a state.
Somebody is in the act of closing it.
The shop was closed down permanently.
exercises.explain: sein + Partizip is the Zustandspassiv: the result, not the event. „wird geschlossen“ would be the closing happening.

exercises.prompt: Das Problem ___ sich leicht lösen.
exercises.explain: sich lassen + Infinitiv is one of the standard passive substitutes — „can be solved“ — and it is far more idiomatic here than „kann gelöst werden“.

exercises.prompt: Why would a report write „Die Entscheidung wurde getroffen“ rather than naming who?
options: To move the action to the front and leave the agent out.
Because the passive is more formal by nature.
Because German has no word for the agent here.
exercises.explain: That is the whole function, and it is also why the passive is worth reading critically: leaving the agent out is a choice.

exercises.prompt: Die Stadt wurde ___ ein Erdbeben zerstört.
exercises.explain: durch for a cause or a means; von for a person or an agent acting deliberately.

exercises.prompt: Das Essen wird von dem Koch gekocht worden.
exercises.fix: Das Essen ist von dem Koch gekocht worden.
exercises.explain: worden belongs to the Perfekt, which takes sein — ist … worden. wird … worden mixes the present and the perfect.

exercises.prompt: Build the passive substitute:
exercises.explain: sein + zu + Infinitiv — „can be avoided“. A third passive substitute beside sich lassen and -bar.
